WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- President Bush has expressed his "deep concern" and regret to Iraq's prime minister over the desecration of a Quran by an American soldier, the White House said Tuesday. President Bush called Nuri al-Maliki over the incident, al-Maliki's office says. The leaders are seen in September. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said Bush spoke to Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki on Monday in one of their regularly scheduled secure video teleconferences. "President Bush expressed his deep concern over the incident and told Prime Minister Maliki that the soldier has been reprimanded by his commanders and removed from Iraq," Johndroe said. Al-Maliki's office on Tuesday said Bush issued an apology for the action on behalf of the United States and "promised to present the soldier to the courts." The office said Bush made the apology in a call to al-Maliki on Tuesday morning. An American staff sergeant -- a sniper section leader -- used a Quran for target practice in Iraq earlier this month. The U.S. commander in Baghdad issued a formal apology Saturday and read a letter of apology by the shooter.  Watch the U.S. military formally apologize » . The sergeant has been relieved of duty as a section leader "with prejudice," officially reprimanded by his commanding general, dismissed from his regiment and redeployed -- reassigned to the United States, the U.S. military said. Reports of the Quran desecration have enraged Muslims in Iraq and elsewhere around the world. The soldier, whose name was not released, shot at a Quran on May 9, villagers said. The Quran used in the incident was discovered two days later, according to the military. A tribal leader said "the criminal act by U.S. forces" took place at a shooting range at the Radhwaniya police station on Baghdad's western outskirts. After the shooters left, an Iraqi policeman found a target marked in the middle of the bullet-riddled Quran. Pictures of the Quran show multiple bullet holes and an expletive scrawled on one of its pages. Officials said the soldier asserted he wasn't aware the book was the Quran, but U.S. officials rejected the claim. On Saturday, Maj. Gen. Jeffery Hammond, commander of U.S. forces in Baghdad, appeared with leaders from Radhwaniya and apologized. "I come before you here seeking your forgiveness," Hammond said to tribal leaders and others at the ceremony. "In the most humble manner I look in your eyes today and I say please forgive me and my soldiers." Hammond also read a letter from the shooter, who called his actions "shortsighted, very reckless and irresponsible," but he insisted he was not being malicious. "I sincerely hope that my actions have not diminished the partnership that our two nations have developed together," the letter said. Hammond said the soldier's actions were tantamount to "criminal behavior." "I've come to this land to protect you, to support you -- not to harm you -- and the behavior of this soldier was nothing short of wrong and unacceptable," the general said. Another military official kissed a Quran and presented it as "a humble gift" to the tribal leaders. Many Iraqi leaders said the apology alone would not suffice.  Watch villagers protest the desecration » . On Monday, the Iraqi Islamic Party, the movement of Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, condemned what it said was a "blatant assault on the sanctities of Muslims all over the world." The party said it reacted to the news "with deep resentment and indignation" and wants the "severest of punishments" for the action. "What truly concerns us is the repetition of these crimes that have happened in the past when mosques were destroyed and pages of the holy Quran were torn and used for disgraceful acts by U.S. soldiers," al-Hashimi said. "I have asked that first this apology be officially documented; second a guarantee from the U.S. military to inflict the maximum possible punishment on this soldier so it would be a deterrent for the rest of the soldiers in the future." CNN's Ed Henry and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Bush has expressed his “deep concern” and regret to Iraq’s prime minister over the desecration of a Quran by an American soldier, the White House said Tuesday.

President Bush called Nuri al-Maliki regarding the incident, according to al-Maliki’s office. The leaders are seen together in September.

National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe said Bush spoke with Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki on Monday during one of their regularly scheduled secure video teleconferences.

“President Bush expressed his deep concern over the incident and told Prime Minister Maliki that the soldier has been reprimanded by his commanders and removed from Iraq,” Johndroe said.

Al-Maliki’s office said Tuesday that Bush issued an apology for the action on behalf of the United States and “promised to present the soldier to the courts.” The office said Bush made the apology during a call to al-Maliki on Tuesday morning.

An American staff sergeant, a sniper section leader, used a Quran for target practice in Iraq earlier this month. The U.S. commander in Baghdad issued a formal apology Saturday and read aloud a letter of apology from the shooter.

The sergeant has been relieved of duty as a section leader “with prejudice,” formally reprimanded by his commanding general, dismissed from his regiment, and redeployed—reassigned to the United States—the U.S. military said.

Reports of the Quran’s desecration have angered Muslims in Iraq and elsewhere around the world. The soldier, whose name has not been released, shot at a Quran on May 9, villagers said. The Quran used in the incident was discovered two days later, according to the military.

A tribal leader said “the criminal act by U.S. forces” took place at a shooting range at the Radhwaniya police station on Baghdad’s western outskirts. After the shooters left, an Iraqi policeman found a target marked in the middle of the bullet-riddled Quran. Pictures of the Quran show multiple bullet holes and an expletive scrawled on one of its pages.

Officials said the soldier asserted that he was unaware the book was the Quran, but U.S. officials rejected that claim.

On Saturday, Maj. Gen. Jeffery Hammond, commander of U.S. forces in Baghdad, appeared with leaders from Radhwaniya and apologized.

“I come before you here seeking your forgiveness,” Hammond told tribal leaders and others at the ceremony. “In the most humble manner, I look in your eyes today and I say: please forgive me and my soldiers.”

Hammond also read a letter from the shooter, who described his actions as “shortsighted, very reckless and irresponsible,” while insisting he had not acted maliciously.

“I sincerely hope that my actions have not diminished the partnership that our two nations have developed together,” the letter said.

Hammond said the soldier’s actions were tantamount to “criminal behavior.”

“I’ve come to this land to protect you, to support you—not to harm you—and the behavior of this soldier was nothing short of wrong and unacceptable,” the general said.

Another military official kissed a Quran and presented it as “a humble gift” to the tribal leaders.

Many Iraqi leaders said the apology alone would not suffice.

On Monday, the Iraqi Islamic Party, the movement of Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, condemned what it called a “blatant assault on the sanctities of Muslims all over the world.” The party said it received the news “with deep resentment and indignation” and called for the “severest of punishments” for the action.

“What truly concerns us is the repetition of these crimes that have happened in the past, when mosques were destroyed and pages of the holy Quran were torn and used for disgraceful acts by U.S. soldiers,” al-Hashimi said.

“I have asked that, first, this apology be officially documented; second, that there be a guarantee from the U.S. military to inflict the maximum possible punishment on this soldier so it would be a deterrent for the rest of the soldiers in the future.”

CNN’s Ed Henry and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

The U.S. military said the sergeant was removed “with prejudice” from his position as section leader, formally reprimanded by his commanding general, dismissed from his regiment and redeployed to the United States.

News of the desecration angered Muslims in Iraq and in other parts of the world.

Villagers said the unnamed soldier fired at the Quran on May 9. Military officials said the Quran involved in the incident was found two days afterward.

A tribal leader said the “criminal act by U.S. forces” occurred at a firing range at the Radhwaniya police station on the western edge of Baghdad. After the shooters had left, an Iraqi police officer discovered a target placed in the center of the Quran, which had been pierced by bullets.

Photographs of the Quran showed several bullet holes and an obscenity written on one of its pages.

Officials said the soldier claimed he did not realize the book was the Quran, but U.S. officials dismissed that explanation.

On Saturday, Maj. Gen. Jeffery Hammond, who commands U.S. forces in Baghdad, stood alongside leaders from Radhwaniya and offered an apology.

“I come before you here seeking your forgiveness,” Hammond told tribal figures and others attending the ceremony. “In the most humble manner I look in your eyes today and I say please forgive me and my soldiers.”

Hammond also read a statement from the soldier who fired on the Quran. In it, the soldier described his conduct as “shortsighted, very reckless and irresponsible,” while maintaining that he did not act out of malice.

“I sincerely hope that my actions have not diminished the partnership that our two nations have developed together,” the letter said.

Hammond described the soldier’s behavior as equivalent to “criminal behavior.”

“I’ve come to this land to protect you, to support you — not to harm you — and the behavior of this soldier was nothing short of wrong and unacceptable,” the general said.

Another U.S. military official kissed a Quran and handed it to tribal leaders as “a humble gift.”

Many Iraqi leaders said an apology by itself was not enough.

On Monday, the Iraqi Islamic Party, associated with Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi, denounced what it called a “blatant assault on the sanctities of Muslims all over the world.”

The party said it received the news “with deep resentment and indignation” and called for the “severest of punishments” over the incident.

“What truly concerns us is the repetition of these crimes that have happened in the past when mosques were destroyed and pages of the holy Quran were torn and used for disgraceful acts by U.S. soldiers,” al-Hashimi said.

He added: “I have asked that first this apology be officially documented; second a guarantee from the U.S. military to inflict the maximum possible punishment on this soldier so it would be a deterrent for the rest of the soldiers in the future.”

A senior U.S. commander in Iraq also issued a formal apology to local tribal leaders, calling the act “criminal behavior” and pledging that it would not be tolerated.

Al-Maliki’s government has repeatedly pressed U.S. officials to show greater sensitivity to Iraqi culture and religious traditions amid ongoing tensions over the American military presence in the country.

The White House said Bush reaffirmed his commitment to the U.S.-Iraq partnership and stressed that the United States would continue working with the Iraqi government to promote stability and security.

Maj. Gen. Jeffery Hammond, then the U.S. commander responsible for forces in Baghdad, personally apologized to Iraqi community leaders during a meeting in the area. He described the soldier’s conduct as “criminal behavior” and said it was the act of one individual, not a reflection of U.S. forces.

“I come before you here seeking your forgiveness,” Hammond told tribal and local leaders, according to accounts of the meeting. U.S. officials also presented a new Quran to the community as part of the apology.

The White House said Bush assured Maliki that the United States took the matter seriously and that the conduct did not represent the values of the American people or the U.S. military.

Iraqi officials and religious leaders strongly condemned the act. Many Iraqis viewed the shooting of the Quran as a profound religious insult, and political figures demanded a clear response from Washington and the U.S. command. The desecration prompted public anger and risked undermining efforts to build trust between American troops and Iraqi communities. U.S. officials moved quickly to contain the fallout, emphasizing that the soldier had acted alone and that disrespect toward Islam would not be tolerated.

The incident became one of several during the Iraq War in which U.S. personnel were accused of religious or cultural misconduct, highlighting the tensions surrounding a foreign military presence in a deeply religious society.
